title: Technical deep dive: autoscaling & capacity planning
summary: Deep technical discussion about capacity planning for HealthFirst's inference workload. Covered autoscaling policies (burst vs reserved), queueing and tail latency effects, KV cache warmup, batching/quantization tradeoffs, and on-prem/VPC deployment constraints. Agreed next steps: run benchmarks with representative prompt set, share security docs, and provide Dedicated pricing and a deployment runbook.
transcript:
Meeting header: 2026-06-15 16:00 PDT | Duration: ~60m | Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Daniel Ortiz (Redwood SE), Sanjay Patel (CTO - HealthFirst), Elena Gomez (Lead ML Engineer), Rita Huang (Infra/SRE)

[00:00] Maya Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, we'll kick off, quick intros, then Daniel will dive into autoscaling and capacity planning, hopes to make this practical not just theory.
[00:22] Sanjay Patel: Yep, thanks. High level we run clinical summarization and alerting models, heavy bursts during business hours, compliance is big, so need VPC/on-prem options and audit logs, right.
[00:40] Daniel Ortiz: Got it, thanks. Quick question before we start — can you share your p95 latency SLO and peak qps numbers? That will guide the sizing.
[00:50] Elena Gomez: Our target p95 is 250ms for short chats, peaks around 600 qps for embedding-ish endpoints but the actual heavy seq gen peaks are like 120 qps with 1k token average. We're seeing big variance when billing cycles and reporting kick in.
[01:10] Rita Huang: And we have a burst window when clinicians run day-end reports, so we want burst capacity but not pay for 24/7 reserved GPUs.
[01:22] Daniel Ortiz: Totally reasonable. We'll talk reserved capacity plus burst policies. At runtime we separate two levers: reserved pools for baseline throughput and burst pools for ephemeral scale. Reserved GPUs reduce cold-start and KV cache misses because the model stays warm.
[01:40] Maya Chen: To add, Redwood offers Reserved/Dedicated pools plus an autoscale group for bursts. The autoscaler can launch smaller VM-backed instances that spin up faster for non-low-latency routes.
[01:55] Sanjay Patel: How do you handle queueing during spikes? We can't let tail latency blow up.
[02:05] Daniel Ortiz: Good question. We use a request queue with priority tiers. Critical real-time routes get higher priority and bypass large queues; lower-priority batch-like requests can queue or be rate-limited. We also support a token-burst policy where short spikes are absorbed by a token bucket up to X seconds.
[02:30] Elena Gomez: Is the queueing behavior configurable per-route? We have some endpoints that can tolerate 2s and some that must be sub-300ms.
[02:38] Daniel Ortiz: Yes per-route SLOs and queueing policy. You can set max queue depth, timeout, and whether to reject vs queue.
[02:48] Rita Huang: Any notes on the impact of batching on latency distribution? We use batching to improve throughput but worried about p95 tail.
[02:58] Daniel Ortiz: Batching is a latency vs cost tradeoff. For short sequence lengths, small micro-batches (2-8) can help and keep p95 within SLOs. For long sequences, batching increases payload time; we recommend dynamic batching with latency caps — the batch will flush at N or after T ms.
[03:20] Sanjay Patel: KV cache — how do cache warmups behave on scale-up? If we spin up new workers during a burst, do they start cold and penalize latency?
[03:30] Daniel Ortiz: Yes, new worker nodes start with cold KV caches. For models with large KV state (long context), cold starts can add 50-200ms depending on sequence length. To mitigate, we provide two strategies: pre-warm (keep a small pool warm even during low load) and distributed prefix caching where cached prefixes are shared among nodes for popular prompts. There's also an option to pin a small reserved pool to keep KV hot for critical routes.
[04:00] Elena Gomez: Sharing caches sounds interesting — is that available on private deployments/VPC?
[04:08] Daniel Ortiz: On hosted we provide cross-node caching primitives. For VPC/on-prem, we ship a cache sync daemon that can run in the cluster; network and security policies are configurable, but sync frequency and size can be tuned for privacy needs.
[04:25] Sanjay Patel: For on-prem we might not want cross-node syncing beyond the cluster, but syncing inside the VPC is fine. Any encryption for cache at rest?
[04:33] Maya Chen: Cache can be encrypted at rest and in transit; for Private deployments we integrate with customer KMS and HSM for keys. We'll share SOC2 and security docs after this call.
[04:45] Rita Huang: Quantization — do quantized models affect cold-start or cache behavior? We're considering int8 to reduce GPU footprint.
[04:55] Daniel Ortiz: Quantization reduces memory and compute, which means you can fit more concurrent streams per GPU, reducing the number of nodes you need. Cold-starts for quantized models are usually faster since smaller weights load quicker, but inference kernel selection can change and sometimes increases per-token latency for certain ops. We recommend evaluating 4-bit and int8 profiles; Redwood Optimize offers recommendations per workload.
[05:20] Elena Gomez: OK, say we want to keep baseline reserved GPUs to cover 60% of median traffic and allow 5x burst. How do you recommend sizing?
[05:30] Daniel Ortiz: Start by profiling typical requests: tokens per request, avg infer time per token on target hardware, and batching gains. A simple formula: required concurrent streams = peak_rps * avg_latency_seconds. Multiply by safety factor (1.2-1.5) and divide by streams_per_gpu (which depends on quant/batch). Then set reserved to cover baseline and configure burst autoscaler with cooldowns and scaling steps to avoid flapping.
[05:55] Sanjay Patel: Can you give a concrete example?
[05:58] Daniel Ortiz: Sure. If peak is 120 qps with avg 1k tokens and mean token-time 6ms token (so 6s per request), concurrency is 120*6 = 720. If a GPU can handle 24 concurrent streams at our chosen quant/batch, you'd need 30 GPUs. Baseline reserved at 40% => 12 GPUs reserved, autoscale up to 30 with burst. These numbers vary a lot with quant and batching.
[06:30] Elena Gomez: That concurrency math helps. What about warm-up time when autoscaler provisions GPUs — minutes or seconds?
[06:38] Daniel Ortiz: For cloud-backed burst pools with pre-built images, warm up is typically 60-180 seconds including model load depending on model size. For on-prem bare-metal you can get faster if you keep preloaded images on a small standby fleet.
[06:55] Rita Huang: If warm-up is that long, we need to avoid p95 spikes. Do you support overprovisioning of a small standby fleet?
[07:03] Maya Chen: Yes, common pattern: keep a tiny hot pool for critical routes and use burst for less critical. Also token-bucket absorbers can buy you seconds to let nodes spin up.
[07:15] Sanjay Patel: What about cost controls? We don't want runaway autoscale during a bad traffic pattern.
[07:22] Daniel Ortiz: You can set max nodes, spend budgets, and automatic fallbacks to cheaper model variants or quantized variants. Redwood's routing layer can route to cheaper models when cost thresholds are hit.
[07:35] Elena Gomez: For VPC/on-prem, is autoscaling limited by our infra? We run on-prem with a private k8s cluster.
[07:43] Daniel Ortiz: In Private setups, autoscaling depends on your cluster autoscaler and available resources. We provide hooks to integrate with cluster autoscalers and can run a controller that prioritizes inference pods. For air-gapped setups, you might prefer reserved sizing and scheduled scale-ups for predictable windows.
[08:00] Sanjay Patel: Any benchmarking we should run?
[08:05] Daniel Ortiz: We'll suggest a benchmark harness: mix of representative prompts (short chat, long seq, embeddings), ramp tests, and spike tests. Include cold-start runs and cache-warm runs. We'll run with quant variants and different batching configs.
[08:20] Maya Chen: Actionable next steps: we'll run a preliminary benchmark with your sample data, send Dedicated pricing and a runbook, and share security docs.
[08:32] Sanjay Patel: Sounds good. Timeline — can we get the bench results within a week? We can provide sample prompts and a small dataset tonight.
[08:42] Daniel Ortiz: Yes, if you provide dataset today we can run baseline bench in 3-5 business days. For deeper on-prem tests might take longer.
[08:55] Elena Gomez: One more question: what telemetry do we get to monitor queue depth and KV cache hit rates?
[09:02] Daniel Ortiz: Redwood Console provides per-route metrics: queue depth, avg/95/99 latency, KV cache hit/miss, batch sizes, per-GPU utilization, and token-level cost breakdown. You can also stream traces to your observability stack.
[09:20] Rita Huang: Great. Any limitations we should be aware of?
[09:25] Daniel Ortiz: For very large model (>70B) cold-starts are longer and memory fragmentation can be a problem on small burst nodes; in those cases we recommend keeping more reserved capacity or using kernel-level sharing via multi-instance GPU.
[09:40] Maya Chen: Recap: Redwood will — 1) run benchmark with provided prompts, 2) share Dedicated pricing and runbook, 3) share SOC2/security pack and deployment notes for VPC, 4) propose an initial reserved/burst sizing draft.
[09:58] Sanjay Patel: Perfect. Let's set a follow-up to review bench results and sizing.
[10:05] Maya Chen: I'll send calendar invite for a follow-up 1 week after we deliver results. Thanks everyone.

Notes: transcript contains some ASR artifacts e.g., "KV cash" at times, occasional speaker overlaps and mislabels.
